text: To espouse an idea or cause is to adopt it as your own and support it openly — the word shares a root with “spouse,” as if you had married the idea. Finland's education leaders espoused play-based learning: they didn't just allow it, they embraced it and promoted it as their official philosophy.

To posit something is to put it forward as a serious claim or explanation that hasn't been proven yet. Finland's critics posit that its famous 2000 results came from old-fashioned teaching, not the progressive methods it preached — an argument offered for debate, not a settled fact.

A scourge is something that causes widespread suffering or damage — originally the word meant a whip. Writers use it for problems that lash whole populations: the scourge of war, of malaria. Here covid and screens are the two scourges that have battered every child's schooling.

Dim literally means giving little light, but applied to a person it means not very intelligent — “dim” and “bright” are opposites for minds as well as lamps. The headline asks whether teenagers are growing dimmer: becoming less capable thinkers, as the falling test scores suggest.

In British English you “sit” an exam — meaning you take it. So tests “sat by 15-year-olds” are tests those students took, and “the latest tests were sat in all 38 OECD member-countries” means students took them there. Nothing to do with chairs.
Marks is the British word for grades or scores — what American students would call their grades. “Marks in mathematics, reading and science had collapsed” means scores in those subjects fell sharply.

A calamity is a disaster — an event causing great damage and distress. The calamity here is the covid pandemic, which shut schools around the world; policymakers hoped that with it “well in the past,” scores would recover.

An aptitude is a natural ability or developed skill at something — what you're capable of doing. PISA measures young people's aptitudes in reading, math and science: not what facts they've memorized, but what they can actually do with what they've learned.

Compulsory means required by rule or law — you have no choice. “Compulsory school days” are the years when the law requires children to attend school; PISA tests 15-year-olds because in most countries that's near the end of required schooling.

To rule the roost is to be the dominant one, in charge of everyone else — the image is the top chicken in the henhouse. Asian school systems rule the roost in PISA: they sit at the top of the rankings, as they have in almost every round since 2000.

To wipe the floor with someone is to defeat them completely and one-sidedly, as if using them as a mop. Children in China wiped the floor with almost everyone else — their scores weren't just better, they were in a different league, about 100 points above the rich-country average.

Skewed means distorted or tilted so it doesn't give a true picture. China's scores are skewed because only four rich provinces take the test — the sample isn't representative of the whole country, so the result looks better than a nationwide test would.

A rule of thumb is a rough, practical guideline that's approximately right without being exact. The rule of thumb here: 20 PISA points equals about one year of learning — not a precise law, but a handy converter for making sense of score gaps.

Heartening means encouraging — news that lifts your spirits and gives you heart. The heartening news is Britain's: its youngsters now rank in the world's top ten in all three subjects while most rich countries slide. The opposite is “disheartening.”

A discipline here is a field of study — reading, mathematics and science are the three disciplines PISA tests. It's a different sense from “a lax approach to discipline” later in the article, where discipline means keeping order and enforcing rules.

Clouded means made unclear or hard to interpret, the way clouds hide the sky. America's findings are clouded by low response rates: too few students took the test properly, so it's hard to be sure what the data really show.

To tumble is to fall suddenly and helplessly — journalists love it for numbers that drop fast. America's literacy scores have tumbled in line with the rich-world trend: they've fallen sharply, just like everyone else's.

A utility bill is the monthly statement charging a household for basic services — electricity, gas, water. It's full of rates, tiers and fees, and the OECD's grim point is that the weakest fifth of 15-year-olds will struggle to make sense of even that everyday document.

Lingering means staying on after it should have gone — a lingering cough outlasts the cold that caused it. The lingering impact of the pandemic is the damage still showing up in test scores years after schools reopened.

Unchecked means not stopped or restrained — nothing is holding it back. (It's from “check” meaning to halt, as in chess, not “check” meaning to verify.) The pandemic created new problems that continue unchecked: like high absence rates, still running wild years later.
Contested means argued over — people dispute it and no one has won the argument. Why school absences remain so high is “much contested”: experts disagree sharply about the reasons.

A fortnight is British English for two weeks — from the old English “fourteen nights.” About 15% of pupils in rich countries now miss at least a day of primary school every fortnight, up from about 10% before covid.

Ubiquitous means present everywhere at once — you can't escape it. Ubiquitous phones means nearly every teenager has one within reach at all times, which the OECD's education chief argues is costing them practice with long, complex texts.

Hasty means done with too much speed and too little care. “Hasty readers” is the OECD's label for test-takers who blast through the reading test quickly while getting many answers wrong — speed without understanding.

To divert something is to turn it away from its original path — traffic, a river, or attention. Screens are diverting children from books: pulling their reading time toward phones, so the share of American nine-year-olds who read for pleasure has fallen from nearly 60% to 37%.

To drop the ball is to fail at your responsibility through carelessness — the image is a fielder muffing an easy catch. Education ministries seem to be dropping the ball: on issue after issue, they're failing to do their job well.

Complacent means so satisfied with yourself that you stop trying to improve — comfort that breeds carelessness. Schools have become complacent, the OECD's education chief worries: content to tell pupils and parents that mediocre work is great.
Mediocre means ordinary, middling, not very good — the polite word for “meh.” The charge is that schools increasingly praise mediocre work as if it were great, which removes any push to do better.

Zealous means intensely enthusiastic; overzealous means so enthusiastic you overdo it and cause harm. The overzealous use of classroom software means schools rushing to adopt educational technology far beyond what the evidence supports.

Haphazard means done without plan or system — scattered, random, hit-or-miss. Schools' use of educational software is haphazard as well as overzealous: not just too much of it, but adopted with no careful method for checking what works.

Crash-test dummies are the human-shaped figures carmakers strap into vehicles and smash into walls to see what would happen to real people. Calling pupils crash-test dummies for unproven software means schools are running the experiment on live children — if the technology fails, the kids absorb the damage.

Kit is British English for equipment or gear — a soldier's kit, sports kit, and here classroom technology. “Unproven kit” means educational software and devices that haven't been shown to actually help children learn.

Rowdy means noisy and disorderly — a rowdy classroom is one where the teacher struggles to keep control. Schools have been allowed to grow rowdier: surveys find teachers spending more and more time simply keeping order instead of teaching.

Something creeping up is increasing slowly and almost unnoticed — the way a cat creeps. The time teachers spend keeping order is creeping up: rising gradually, survey by survey, without any single dramatic jump.

Dodgy is British slang for unreliable, suspect, probably wrong — a dodgy deal, a dodgy internet connection. A dodgy course here is a mistaken direction: PISA itself may have sent school reformers the wrong way by crowning Finland in 2000.

To trek is to make a long, effortful journey — the word comes from Afrikaans, for grueling ox-wagon migrations. Policymakers trekked to Helsinki: education officials from around the world made pilgrimages to Finland to learn its secret.

The establishment is the group of powerful insiders who run a field and share its orthodox views — the educational establishment means the professors, officials and experts who dominate education. It's often slightly barbed, hinting they protect fashionable ideas from challenge.

Prevalent means widespread and common in a particular place or time. Old-fashioned teaching methods were still prevalent in Finland's schools well into the 1990s — still the norm in most classrooms, whatever the country's spokesmen preached.

In education, progressive doesn't mean politically liberal — it names a century-old movement holding that children learn best through play, projects and discovering things themselves rather than direct teaching and testing. Finland became famous for progressive policies; its critics now argue those policies never earned the credit.

Fanatical means devoted to something with extreme, single-minded intensity. Parents in East Asia are fanatical about schooling: education dominates family life, and many pay heavily for extra lessons on top of the school day.

To dig deep into your pockets is to spend a lot of your own money, often more than is comfortable. East Asian parents dig deep for tutoring and cram schools — private spending on education far beyond what the state provides.

To replicate something is to copy it exactly and make it happen again somewhere else. Critics say East Asia's fanatical schooling culture is difficult to replicate — a Western country can copy Asian policies, but not the social attitudes behind them.

From “zigzag”: to zig when everyone else zags is to deliberately go the opposite way from the crowd. England's school reformers zigged when the world zagged — they toughened exams and packed curriculums with facts just as other countries moved toward softer, trendier approaches.

A coalition government is one where two or more parties share power because no single party won a majority — common in Europe, rare in Britain. The Conservative-led coalition of 2010–15 (Conservatives plus Liberal Democrats) is when England's school reforms began.

Knowledge-rich is the label for curriculums built around a demanding core of facts — dates, formulas, vocabulary, science content — on the theory that you can't think critically about things you don't know. It's the deliberate opposite of teaching general “skills” with little fixed content.

To wax lyrical about something is to talk about it with growing, gushing enthusiasm — “wax” is an old verb meaning to grow, as in a waxing moon. Policymakers elsewhere were waxing lyrical about soft skills: rhapsodizing about them while England doubled down on facts.

Soft skills are general personal abilities — communication, teamwork, creativity, adaptability — as opposed to “hard,” testable knowledge like algebra or chemistry. The article calls them vague: many curriculums promised to instill them without defining what exactly would be taught or how anyone would know it worked.

To instill something in someone is to plant it in their mind gradually, drop by drop — the Latin root literally means to drip in. Curriculums promised to instill soft skills in pupils: to slowly build habits like teamwork and creativity into them.
Rigorous means strict, thorough and demanding, with no corners cut. England made its exams more rigorous — harder to pass and harder to game — as part of its back-to-basics reforms.

To deprioritise something (British spelling of deprioritize) is to push it down the list of what matters. England deprioritised coursework — assignments done at home that count toward final grades — largely because coursework is easy to cheat on.

In the British system, coursework is graded work done during the school year — essays and projects completed outside exam conditions that count toward the final qualification. England pushed it aside in favor of final exams, partly because work done at home is easy to cheat on.

Newfangled describes something new in a way the speaker distrusts — trendy, gimmicky, unproven. England steered schools away from newfangled styles of instruction that were fashionable but untested, back toward older methods with a track record.

Dyed-in-the-wool means thoroughly, permanently of a kind — wool dyed before being spun holds its color forever, so a dyed-in-the-wool fan is a fan through and through. Here it describes traditional teaching methods: deeply established, time-tested ways of running a classroom.

Stark means harsh, plain and unmistakable, so a starkly different path is one that differs sharply — no subtle shading. Scotland chose a starkly different path from England's: a trendier curriculum and looser discipline instead of facts and rigorous exams.

For an American reader this phrase usually means Mexico — but the border here is Scotland's border with England. Scottish children once outperformed “their peers south of the border,” meaning English children; now the ranking has flipped.

Modish means fashionable — in the current mode — and it usually carries a sneer: trendy rather than good. Scotland's critics blame a modish curriculum, one built on fashionable educational ideas instead of proven ones.
Lax means loose, slack, not strict enough — lax security, lax rules. A lax approach to discipline means Scottish schools are accused of letting misbehavior slide rather than enforcing order.

A disparity is a notable gap or difference between two things that might be expected to match. The disparity here is between Scotland's results and England's — a gap that can't be blamed on covid or screens, since both hit all of Britain's children similarly.
Fat, applied to money, means large — a fat paycheck, a fat profit. Fatter earnings simply means higher pay: good grades strongly predict earning more later in life.

In economics, returns are what you get back on something you put money or effort into — the payoff on an investment. The returns on a top-class education are the extra earnings and opportunities it buys; the article sees no sign yet that AI is shrinking them.

To make mincemeat of someone is to destroy them utterly — mincemeat being meat chopped to shreds. The warning: AI will make mincemeat of the weakly skilled, out-competing workers without a solid education for whatever jobs remain.

To hit the books is to get down to serious studying. The article's closing line turns it on the adults: it's the school-reformers who need to hit the books — to study what actually works and fix their systems.

To plumb is to measure how deep something goes, from the lead weight (“plumb bob”) sailors lowered to sound the seabed. Scores that could “plumb further depths” would sink to new lows — the set phrase is usually “plumb the depths.”

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development — a club of 38 mostly rich democracies that collects statistics and compares policies so members can learn from each other. It runs the PISA tests and publishes much of the world's most-cited economic and education data.

The Programme for International Student Assessment — the OECD's test of reading, math and science, sat every three years by 15-year-olds in dozens of countries. Because everyone takes the same test at the same age, it works as a league table for the world's school systems.

A league table is a ranking from best to worst — the term comes from sports leagues, where teams are listed by wins. Britain uses it for any published ranking: of schools, hospitals, universities. PISA results form an international league table of school systems.

Gross domestic product — the total value of everything a country produces in a year, the standard measure of the size of its economy. One analysis says raising PISA scores by 25 points could add half a percentage point to annual GDP growth in rich countries: smarter students, richer economies.
say: gee-dee-PEE, saying the three letters G, D, P

text: A percentage point is the unit of difference between two percentages: going from 2% growth to 2.5% is a rise of half a percentage point (though it's actually a 25% increase in the growth rate). Economists say “percentage point” precisely because “percent” would be ambiguous — and half a point of extra GDP growth, compounded over decades, is enormous.

The section heading's grammar mistake is a deliberate joke: it quotes George W. Bush, who famously asked in 2000, “Rarely is the question asked: is our children learning?” The garbled question became shorthand for worries about educational standards — which is exactly this article's subject.

Play-based learning builds lessons around games, free play and exploration instead of direct instruction, on the theory that young children learn naturally through play. Finland championed it, especially for younger children — and its steep score decline has put the approach under harsh new scrutiny.

On the contrary flatly rejects what came before and asserts the opposite. Hopes were that scores would rebound; on the contrary — they fell further. It's stronger than “however”: not just a different point, but the reverse of what was expected.
